title: Mutation Testing in Python with Cosmic Ray - Austin Bingham - NDC TechTown 2024
summary: Austin Bingham explains mutation testing theory, its practical obstacles (runtime, equivalent mutants, unreachable code) and demonstrates the Cosmic Ray tool for Python.

assertions.quote: it's not really telling you that your tests are that you understand what your program is doing

verdicts.note: Well established; Inozemtseva and Holmes found coverage only weakly correlates with suite effectiveness once suite size is controlled.

Across 31,000 generated suites on five large Java systems, coverage correlated only low-to-moderately with mutation-detection effectiveness once suite size was controlled, so high coverage does not indicate an effective suite; executing a line does not reveal an error in it.

assertions.quote: the quality of your tests can be gauged by the percentage of mutations killed

verdicts.note: Just et al. found mutant detection correlates with real-fault detection, with caveats about mutant representativeness.

The study uses mutation score as its ground-truth measure of fault-detection effectiveness and finds coverage tracks it only weakly; the authors suggest mutation score as a substitute for coverage, but this is their judgment, not a head-to-head test against real faults.

assertions.quote: your tests are inadequate to protect this change this Behavior modifying change or the code that was mutated is extraneous

verdicts.note: Follows from the technique, with the third possibility of an equivalent mutant that the speaker also acknowledges.

A surviving mutant may be an equivalent mutant (e.g. == changed to >= with identical behaviour) rather than a missing test, and manual inspection is needed to tell; the study classified up to 35% of mutants as equivalent, so the either/or omits a third case.

assertions.quote: it is just not practical to do on a frequent basis

verdicts.note: Runtime is the documented adoption barrier; Google's deployment runs mutation analysis only on changed lines for this reason.

assertions.quote: it is not really detectable in any practical way

verdicts.note: Equivalent mutant detection is undecidable in general; heuristics and compiler-based detection remove some but not all.

Manual inspection is required because automatically determining whether a mutant is equivalent is undecidable, which is why studies fall back on assuming anything the master suite misses is equivalent.

assertions.quote: when I have higher level tests that tests my functionality that that is probably one of the keys to Breaking the time barrier

verdicts.note: A practitioner hunch; fewer larger tests may run slower per mutant, so the net effect on runtime is unclear.

assertions.quote: good testing results in better design almost always in my experience
that's actually relatively easy to get if you're if you're motivated to do it

verdicts.note: Achievable for many codebases but costly for legacy or hardware-bound code; coverage-driven tests are often weak, which is the speaker's own point.

Authors call extremely high coverage very difficult to reach, and even their five actively developed Java projects with 600-8,000 test methods sit at 27-76% statement coverage; no motivated team pushing for 100% was studied.
